Nutritional rickets & osteomalacia: A practical approach to management.
Uday S(1), Högler W(2).
(1)Department of Endocrinology & Diabetes, Birmingham Women's & Children's NHS
Foundation Trust; Institute of Metabolism & Systems Research, University of
Birmingham, Edgbaston, Birmingham, UK.
(2)Institute of Metabolism & Systems Research, University of Birmingham,
Edgbaston, Birmingham, UK; Department of Paediatrics & Adolescent Medicine,
Johannes Kepler University, Kepler University Hospital, Med Campus IV, Linz,
Defective mineralization of the growth plate and preformed osteoid result in
rickets and osteomalacia, respectively. The leading cause of rickets worldwide
is solar vitamin D deficiency and/or dietary calcium deficiency collectively
termed as nutritional rickets. Vitamin D deficiency predominates in
high-latitude countries in at-risk groups (dark skin, reduced sun exposure,
infants and pregnant and lactating women) but is emerging in some tropical
countries due to sun avoidance behaviour. Calcium deficiency predominates in
tropical countries, especially in the malnourished population. Nutritional
rickets can have devastating health consequences beyond bony deformities
(swollen wrist and ankle joints, rachitic rosary, soft skull, stunting and
bowing) and include life-threatening hypocalcaemic complications of seizures
and, in infancy, heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy. In children,
diagnosis of rickets (always associated with osteomalacia) is confirmed on
radiographs (cupping and flaring of metaphyses) and should be suspected in high
risk individuals with the above clinical manifestations in the presence of
abnormal blood biochemistry (high alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone,
low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and calcium and/or low phosphate). In adults or
adolescents with closed growth plates, osteomalacia presents with non-specific
symptoms (fatigue, malaise and muscle weakness) and abnormal blood biochemistry,
but only in extreme cases, it is associated with radiographic findings of
Looser's zone fractures. Bone biopsies could confirm osteomalacia at earlier
disease stages, for definitive diagnosis. Treatment includes high-dose
cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol daily for a minimum of 12 wk or stoss therapy
in exceptional circumstances, each followed by lifelong maintenance
supplementation. In addition, adequate calcium intake through diet or
supplementation should be ensured. Preventative approaches should be tailored to
the population needs and incorporate multiple strategies including targeted
vitamin D supplementation of at-risk groups and food fortification with vitamin
D and/or calcium. Economically, food fortification is certainly the most
cost-effective way forward.

INTRODUCTION: We aimed to describe the prevalence of vitamin D deficiency among
American Indian adolescents and determine its association with cardiovascular
disease (CVD) risk factors.
METHODS: Our study population consisted of 307 adolescents (aged ≤20 years)
participating in the Strong Heart Family Study with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D
(25[OH]D) measured on samples collected during baseline examinations
(2001-2003). We defined baseline prevalence of vitamin D deficiency as 25(OH)D
≤20 ng/mL. We evaluated outcomes related to obesity (BMI, waist circumference,
wait-to-hip ratio, and body fat percentage), diabetes, cholesterol, and
metabolic syndrome. We used generalized estimating equations to determine
whether the prevalence of the outcomes differed according to vitamin D
deficiency status, while controlling for covariates. To determine incidence, we
conducted a follow-up examination a median 5.8 years after baseline (2006-2009)
and a second follow-up a median of 13.3 years after baseline (2014-2018). We
calculated incidence rates (IR) per 100 person-years for the total group and
stratified by vitamin D deficiency status at baseline. Finally we used shared
frailty cox proportional hazards models to determine if the risk of the outcomes
differed according to vitamin D deficiency status, while controlling for
RESULTS: The prevalence of vitamin D deficiency was 50.8% at baseline, and it
was associated with the prevalence of obesity, low HDL-C, and metabolic
syndrome, while controlling for covariates. By the first follow-up, the IRs per
100 person-years were the following: obesity (5.03), diabetes (1.07), any
dyslipidemia (10.80), and metabolic syndrome (3.31). By the second follow-up,
the IR of diabetes was significantly higher among those with (vs without)
baseline vitamin D deficiency (1.32 vs 0.68 per 100 person-years; P = .02),
although the association was not significant after adjusting for covariates.
CONCLUSION: Vitamin D deficiency in adolescence may be associated with the CVD
risk factors obesity, low HDL-C, and metabolic syndrome and may also contribute

METHODS: It is a prospective observational study including 150 practicing
orthopaedic surgeons from entire India who visited our centre during 3 months
duration for various educational meetings. Venous sample was collected after due
informed consent and analysed at a single laboratory for 25-OH Cholecalciferol
levels by a chemiluminescent assay. All the samples were analysed and a
questionnaire was sent to the participants via google forms regarding various
parameters under study.
RESULTS: The mean serum Vitamin D levels were 18.6 ± 9.67 ng/ml in the sample
studied. 17 out of 150 participants (11.3%) were found to have sufficient serum
levels of 25(OH) Cholecalciferol. 105 participants (70%) were having deficient
levels and 28 (18.7%) had insufficient levels of Vitamin D. Overall 88.7%
participants had Vitamin D deficiency among the sample studied.
CONCLUSION: This widespread prevalence of Vitamin D deficiency warrants frequent
screening and routine supplementation of Vitamin D in orthopaedic surgeons
thereby providing a low cost solution to improve the troublesome situation among
healthcare providers.

Vitamin D Deficiency and Oxidative Stress in Type 2 Diabetic Population of
Dhas Y, Mishra N(1), Banerjee J.

Vitamin D deficiency is common in metropolitan cities of India and worldwide due
to faulty life style. The prevalence of vitamin D deficiency has tremendously
increased in India despite the fact that it is located between 8.4° and 37.6°
north latitude and majority of the Indian population exposed to ample sunlight
throughout the year. From published data regarding vitamin D deficiency in India
estimated prevalence of vitamin D deficiency is 70%-100% in the adult
population. The main identified reason for vitamin D deficiency is the lack of
appropriate sunlight exposure and no consumption (in case of vegetarian
population) or less consumption of vitamin D containing diet (e.g. fish, cod
liver oil, beef liver and eggs). Mild to moderate vitamin D deficiency is
identified as a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, due to its protective role
against development of type 2 diabetes mellitus and its complications. Vitamin D
may affect glucose homeostasis through increasing insulin resistance and
reducing insulin secretion from beta cells of the pancreas. Vitamin D plays an
important role against oxidative stress, because of its antioxidant property.
Till date very few studies determined the link between vitamin D and oxidative
stress in type 2 diabetes mellitus and its complications. However, more studies
are needed to evaluate an underlying mechanism of vitamin D in amelioration of
the oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

A social media post suggests that drinking jeera water can help melt away belly fat. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
An Instagram post circulating online suggests that drinking jeera tea can melt belly fat.
No. Belly fat does not “melt” because of one drink, one spice, or one morning ritual. The body loses fat gradually when there is a sustained calorie deficit, along with better food choices, movement, sleep, and consistency. Health authorities also note that supplements and herbal products marketed for quick weight loss generally do not produce meaningful long-term results.
The idea sounds attractive because jeera, or cumin, is a familiar kitchen ingredient and is often linked with digestion. But digestion support and fat burning are not the same thing. Even when weight loss happens, the body decides where fat comes off from first. You cannot command it to remove fat only from the stomach area. That is why claims such as “melt belly fat” are more marketing language than medical reality.
We spoke to Chaitali Bharatia, MSc (Specialised Dietetics in Diabetes and Cardiac Nutrition), Senior Nutritionist at Balance Nutrition, to understand whether jeera water can help reduce belly fat. She explains, “Jeera water may have certain health benefits, such as supporting digestion and slightly improving metabolism. However, it should not be viewed as a miracle remedy for weight loss. At present, there is limited scientific evidence to show that jeera water alone can directly reduce or melt belly fat. When used alongside a balanced diet, regular physical activity, and a healthy lifestyle, it may contribute modestly to overall weight management. It is always advisable to consult a healthcare professional before making major dietary changes. In short, while jeera may support weight loss efforts, it cannot work as a standalone solution.”
Dermatologist Dr Jyothy Kannangath highlights that there are no instant or magical solutions for reducing belly fat. According to her, the most reliable ways to address excess abdominal fat include long-term lifestyle changes such as healthy eating and regular physical activity. In certain cases, medical procedures like liposuction or cryolipolysis may also be considered.
We have also previously examined several claims circulating online which suggest that drinking a decoction made from cumin, carom seeds, and cinnamon can remove belly fat without any need for diet control or exercise. However, these claims are misleading and lack strong scientific evidence.
Can cumin help a little when paired with an overall weight-loss plan?
Yes. Some small clinical trials suggest cumin may have a modest supportive effect in certain people, but that is very different from saying jeera tea melts fat. In one trial of 88 overweight or obese women, those given 3 grams of cumin powder daily with yoghurt, along with the same weight-loss counselling as the control group, had reductions in weight, BMI, waist circumference, and fat mass over three months.
Another small eight-week trial reported that cumin capsules led to about 1.1 kg weight loss compared with a slight gain in the placebo group. But this study has an important caution attached to it: PubMed flags it with an expression of concern, which means the findings should be interpreted carefully rather than treated as solid proof.
So, the most honest reading is this: cumin may possibly play a small supporting role in some settings, but the evidence is limited, short-term, and not strong enough to justify dramatic social media promises.
Does jeera tea work the same way as cumin powder or capsules used in studies?
No. This is where many online claims quietly skip an important detail. The studies people often cite did not test a random homemade cup of jeera tea as a stand-alone belly-fat remedy. They used measured amounts of cumin powder or capsules, sometimes with supervised diet advice, and followed participants for only a short period.
That matters. A light infusion made at home may not deliver the same amount or form of active compounds. So even if cumin shows a modest effect in research, it does not automatically mean your daily jeera tea will reproduce it.
What is a more truthful way to think about jeera tea?
Yes, it can be part of a healthy routine, but not as a miracle fix. Jeera tea may be a low-calorie replacement for sugary drinks, and that alone can be useful. If someone swaps sweetened tea, juice, or soft drinks for plain jeera tea, total calorie intake may fall over time. That can support weight management indirectly. But the benefit comes from the overall habit change, not from the tea magically burning stomach fat.
In simple words: jeera tea is fine as a supportive drink, not a belly-fat cure. The claim overpromises what science can actually support. Real fat loss is slower, less glamorous, and much more dependent on daily patterns than on any single cup.

A social media post shows a man loudly claiming that he has so much confidence in his drink made with Eno, lemon, black salt and black pepper that it can even dissolve rocks when consumed. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
A Facebook post claims that mixing lemon juice with Eno, black pepper (kali mirch), and black salt (kala namak) creates a powerful drink capable of helping with indigestion. The claimant even exaggerate further, saying that “even if someone eats rocks, this drink will digest them”.
Can this drink actually dissolve rocks if consumed?
No. There is absolutely no scientific basis for the idea that this drink can dissolve rocks in the human body. Rocks are made of hard minerals such as silica, calcium compounds, or other geological materials that require extremely strong acids or high temperatures to break down. The human digestive system simply does not function in that way. Even stomach acid, which is quite strong, cannot dissolve stones or rocks.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid with a pH of around 1.5 to 3.5. This acid helps break down food, especially proteins, but it is not capable of dissolving solid mineral rocks. In fact, if someone were to swallow a rock, the body would not “digest” it at all. It would either pass through the digestive tract or potentially cause injury or blockage.
The ingredients in the viral drink do not change this reality. Lemon juice contains citric acid, but it is far weaker than stomach acid. Eno is mainly a mixture of sodium bicarbonate and citric acid that produces fizz when mixed with water. Black pepper and black salt mainly add flavour and may stimulate digestion slightly, but they do not possess any stone-dissolving properties.
So the idea that this mixture could digest rocks is simply impossible from a biological and chemical perspective.
Dietitian Shikha Sharma, MSc in Foods and Nutrition, Noida, explains, “The claim that a mixture of lemon juice, Eno, black pepper and black salt can dissolve rocks inside the human body has no scientific basis. The digestive system is designed to break down nutrients from food such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats, not solid mineral materials. Even the stomach’s own acid, hydrochloric acid, which is quite strong, cannot dissolve stones or rocks. Lemon juice contains citric acid, but it is significantly weaker than stomach acid, and Eno mainly creates a fizzing reaction due to the release of carbon dioxide gas when its ingredients react with water. This bubbling may look dramatic, but it does not mean the mixture has any ability to break down or dissolve hard substances inside the body.”
Does the fizzing reaction mean it is dissolving something inside the body?
No. The fizz you see when lemon juice and Eno are mixed is just a simple chemical reaction producing carbon dioxide gas. When sodium bicarbonate (in Eno) reacts with acid, bubbles form. This is the same reaction that happens when baking soda is mixed with vinegar in school science experiments. The bubbles may look dramatic, but they do not indicate that anything powerful is happening inside the body.
Once consumed, this reaction quickly settles in the stomach. The fizzing may temporarily relieve acidity by neutralising some stomach acid, which is why products like Eno are sometimes used for indigestion. But the effect is mild and short-lived.
Importantly, the bubbles have nothing to do with dissolving stones or breaking down hard materials. The reaction simply releases gas and forms salts and water. It does not produce any compound capable of dissolving rocks or mineral deposits.
Does this home remedy actually help with digestion?
Yes, but only to a limited extent. Some ingredients in this mixture may provide mild relief from temporary digestive discomfort.
Eno acts as an antacid. Its sodium bicarbonate content can neutralise excess stomach acid, which may help relieve symptoms such as acidity, bloating, or heartburn for a short period. Lemon juice may stimulate saliva and digestive secretions, which can sometimes make people feel that digestion is improving.
Black pepper contains a compound called piperine that can stimulate digestive enzymes and may support the breakdown of food. Similarly, black salt is traditionally used in small amounts in digestive preparations because it may help reduce gas and improve flavour.
However, this does not mean the drink “boosts digestion dramatically” or treats digestive disorders. Its effect is temporary and largely related to acidity relief rather than true digestive improvement. Regular digestive problems should always be evaluated by a healthcare professional rather than relying on home remedies alone.
Dr Durga Priyadarshini, PhD, Nutrition Researcher & Founder, Nutrition Research Hub, Chennai, says “Some ingredients in this mixture may provide mild relief from temporary digestive discomfort. Eno works as an antacid that can neutralise excess stomach acid for a short period, and black pepper contains compounds that may stimulate digestive enzymes. However, this effect is limited and should not be confused with the ability to dissolve stones or rocks. Viral claims often exaggerate simple digestive remedies and present them as powerful cures, which can mislead people. Good digestive health is supported through balanced eating, fibre intake, hydration and medical guidance when needed not through home remedies that promise unrealistic results.”
So this viral claim that lemon juice, Eno, black pepper, and black salt can dissolve rocks inside the body is scientifically impossible. The fizzing reaction in the drink may look impressive, but it does not translate into any stone-dissolving ability inside the human body.
At best, this mixture may offer temporary relief from acidity. At worst, exaggerated claims like these create false hope and spread confusion about how the body actually works.
When it comes to stones or digestive health, reliable medical advice, not viral remedies, remains the safest path.

A social media post suggests that drinking fresh pineapple juice helps get rid of intestinal worms. We fact checked and found the claim to be mostly false.
A social media account named Salatubpune shared a video in which a nutritionist claims that drinking fresh pineapple juice can help eliminate intestinal worms.
Does pineapple juice “kill worms” inside the human gut?
No. There isn’t good clinical evidence that pineapple juice can cure intestinal worm infections in humans. Here’s why this claim sounds believable: pineapple contains proteolytic (protein-breaking) enzymes, and researchers have explored whether plant enzymes can damage worms. In fact, older observations and later scientific reviews describe fresh pineapple juice/extract having effects against certain parasites under laboratory conditions.
But lab conditions are controlled: worms are directly exposed to concentrated juice or purified enzymes for long periods. In real life, once you drink pineapple juice, it gets diluted, mixed with food, and exposed to stomach acid and digestive processes. That makes “worm-killing” inside a human intestine far less predictable.
Dr Sukrit Singh Sethi, Director & Senior Consultant, Gastroenterology, Narayana Hospital, Gurugram, says, “Pineapple juice cannot treat intestinal worm infections. The idea comes from bromelain, an enzyme in pineapple that can damage parasites in laboratory studies and some animal research. However, in humans, stomach acid breaks down bromelain before it reaches the intestines, so it does not work as a deworming treatment. If symptoms like persistent stomach discomfort, diarrhea, weight loss, or visible worms in stool occur, a stool test and medical consultation are necessary. Doctors usually prescribe antiparasitic medicines such as Albendazole or Mebendazole, which are safe and effective.”
So, pineapple juice might be an interesting research lead, but it’s not a dependable deworming treatment.
Most research showing pineapple’s antiparasitic activity has been conducted either in laboratory experiments or in animals such as mice, goats, and poultry.
There is currently no strong clinical evidence showing that pineapple juice can reliably eliminate intestinal worms in humans. Standard anti-parasitic medicines like albendazole or mebendazole remain the medically recommended treatment.
Is bromelain the reason people think pineapple can deworm?
Yes. Bromelain is the main reason pineapple gets linked to “killing parasites.” Bromelain is a group of enzymes found in pineapple (especially the stem and fruit). Scientific work on “plant-derived cysteine proteinases” (a category that includes enzymes like bromelain) suggests these enzymes can damage the outer surface of some worms, reducing their movement or viability in experimental settings.
There are also animal and veterinary studies exploring bromelain-based preparations against gastrointestinal worms (for example, in goats). That’s useful research, but it doesn’t automatically translate into a safe, effective home remedy for humans.
Does it matter if the pineapple juice is fresh, packaged, or heated?
Yes. Processing can matter a lot. One reason “pineapple juice kills worms” became popular is the idea that fresh pineapple juice may contain more active enzymes. Heat can reduce enzyme activity, so some sources note that heated/canned pineapple products may not have the same enzyme effect.
Even so, “fresh is better” doesn’t solve the bigger problem: we still don’t have solid human clinical proof that fresh pineapple juice clears intestinal worms. It’s also not clear what amount would be needed, or whether that amount would be tolerable (pineapple can be acidic and may trigger reflux or mouth irritation in some people).
If pineapple juice isn’t a cure, what does work for intestinal worms?
Previously, we have examined several claims suggesting that remedies like cloves or pumpkin seeds can kill intestinal worms. However, the evidence consistently shows that standard deworming medicines remain the most effective and medically recommended treatment for intestinal worm infections.
For common soil-transmitted worms, public health guidance supports treatment with medicines like albendazole or mebendazole in appropriate doses. The World Health Organization recommends these medicines for deworming programmes in endemic settings, and the CDC provides clinical dosing guidance for different worm infections.
The key point: different worms need different approaches, and some symptoms that people blame on “worms” (bloating, tummy upset, fatigue) can have other causes. If symptoms are persistent, it’s worth getting a proper evaluation rather than guessing.
Dr Anusha Dewan, General Physician at Jeevan Anmol Hospital in Mayur Vihar, New Delhi, explains that intestinal worm infections are best treated with doctor-prescribed antiparasitic medicines such as albendazole or mebendazole, which effectively kill the worms and help the body eliminate them. She adds that good hygiene practices, including regular handwashing, proper cooking of food, and keeping nails short, are essential to prevent reinfection.
In some cases, the dose may be repeated after two weeks, especially for threadworms, while more severe infections may require medicines like ivermectin or praziquantel. The World Health Organization also supports deworming programmes, particularly in areas where these infections are common among children.

A social media post suggests that eating fruits on an empty stomach does not cause a spike in blood sugar levels. We factchecked and found the claim to be false.
An Instagram post claims that eating fruits on an empty stomach does not affect blood sugar levels.
Do fruits eaten on an empty stomach still raise blood sugar?
Yes. Any food containing carbohydrates can affect blood sugar, and fruit is no exception. Whole fruits contain natural sugars, so after eating them, blood glucose can rise. The real question is not whether fruit affects blood sugar at all, but how much and how fast. That depends on the type of fruit, the portion size, its ripeness, and whether it is eaten whole or as juice.
The phrase “empty stomach” can make the claim sound scientific, but it does not cancel out the body’s normal response to carbohydrates. When fruit is eaten alone, there is no magic switch that prevents sugar absorption. The sugars are still digested and absorbed into the bloodstream. What changes is the speed and size of the rise, which varies from fruit to fruit.
Does whole fruit behave differently from fruit juice?
Yes. Whole fruit and fruit juice are not the same when it comes to blood sugar. Whole fruit contains fibre, which helps slow digestion and sugar absorption. Juice, on the other hand, removes or breaks down much of that fibre, so the sugar is absorbed more quickly. That is why public health guidance generally recommends choosing whole fruit over juice.
This is also why juice is often described as causing a faster blood sugar rise than whole fruit. Even when the sugar comes from fruit, the body responds differently to a glass of juice than to chewing an orange or eating an apple. In simple terms, whole fruit is usually the steadier option.
Does eating fruit alone make the blood sugar rise faster?
Often, yes. Eating fruit by itself may lead to a quicker rise in blood sugar than eating it with foods that contain protein, fat, or extra fibre. According to the CDC, carbohydrates raise blood sugar, and pairing them with protein, fat, or fibre can slow how quickly that rise happens.
That does not mean fruit alone is “bad.” It simply means context matters. A banana eaten by itself may affect blood sugar differently from a banana eaten with nuts or yoghurt. The fruit still has nutritional value, but the rest of the meal can shape the blood sugar response.
Dietitian Shikha Sharma, MSc in Foods and Nutrition, Noida says “People often assume that because fruit is natural, it has no effect on blood sugar when eaten on an empty stomach. That is not accurate. Fruits still contain carbohydrates, and those carbohydrates are converted into glucose during digestion. The difference is that whole fruits also provide fibre, which usually slows down the rise in blood sugar compared to sugary drinks or desserts.”
Should people avoid fruit because of its sugar content?
No. Whole fruit should not be confused with sweets, syrups, or sugary drinks. NHS guidance notes that the sugar naturally present in intact fruit is not classed the same way as “free sugars” found in juice or added sugar products. Fruit also provides fibre, vitamins, and other beneficial compounds.
Research does not support the idea that whole fruit should be routinely avoided for blood sugar control. In fact, reviews suggest that fruit intake is not harmful in the way many people fear, and may even support better long-term metabolic health when eaten as part of a balanced diet.
Sakshi Singh, Dietitian, MSc (Food and Nutrition) said, “Eating fruit on an empty stomach does not eliminate the natural sugars present in it. The body will still absorb these sugars. However, whole fruits contain fibre, water, and beneficial plant compounds that slow down how quickly the sugar enters the bloodstream, which is why fruits are generally considered a healthier source of carbohydrates. Pairing fruit with a small portion of protein or healthy fat such as nuts, yoghurt, or seeds—can further slow sugar absorption and help keep blood sugar levels more stable.”
What is the correct takeaway from this claim?
The claim is misleading. Fruits eaten on an empty stomach can affect blood sugar levels. The more accurate message is that whole fruits usually raise blood sugar more slowly and less sharply than fruit juice or highly processed sugary foods, especially because of their fibre content.
So, fruit is not “free” of blood sugar effects, but it is also not the enemy. For most people, the smarter focus is on choosing whole fruit, watching portions when needed, and being mindful of what it is eaten with rather than believing that an empty stomach somehow makes fruit sugar invisible to the body.

A social media post suggest that drinking ginger tea can help melt body fat. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
An Instagram post suggests that drinking ginger tea can “melt fat like a candle,” meaning that body fat rapidly dissolves simply by consuming this drink.
Can ginger tea literally melt fat in the body like a candle?
No, body fat does not melt in the human body the way candle wax melts with heat. The idea that fat can “melt” simply by drinking a warm beverage is a misunderstanding of how the human body works. Body fat is stored in specialised cells called adipocytes, and it cannot simply dissolve because a certain drink or food is consumed. Fat loss happens through a complex metabolic process called lipolysis, in which stored fat molecules are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol. These components are then transported through the bloodstream and used by the body’s cells to produce energy.
For lipolysis to occur in a meaningful way, the body must be in a calorie deficit, meaning it uses more energy than it consumes through food and beverages. Hormones such as adrenaline, glucagon, and insulin regulate this process. If energy intake exceeds expenditure, the body stores excess energy as fat rather than breaking it down.
Therefore, comparing fat loss to candle melting is scientifically inaccurate. No single drink , including ginger tea, can bypass these mechanisms or cause fat to rapidly disappear.
Does ginger contain compounds that influence metabolism or fat burning?
Yes, ginger contains bioactive compounds that may have mild metabolic effects, but these effects are modest and not dramatic. Ginger contains several biologically active substances, particularly gingerols and shogaols, which have been studied for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Some research suggests that these compounds may slightly increase thermogenesis, which is the body’s process of producing heat by burning calories.
A small human study published in the journal Metabolism in 2012 found that ginger consumption increased the thermic effect of food and promoted feelings of satiety after meals. Participants who consumed ginger reported feeling fuller and experienced a slight increase in energy expenditure compared with those who did not consume it.
However, the increase in calorie burning observed in these studies was relatively small. It is nowhere near the level required to produce visible fat loss without changes in overall diet and lifestyle. In other words, ginger may support metabolism in a subtle way, but it cannot trigger rapid or dramatic fat reduction on its own.
Researchers also emphasise that these benefits occur when ginger is consumed as part of a balanced diet, not as a standalone “fat-melting” remedy.
Is there any single drink that can independently cause rapid fat loss?
No. Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda, explains that in Ayurveda, obesity is considered a complex and challenging condition. There is no beverage that can independently trigger significant fat loss in the body. Despite many viral claims online about “fat-burning drinks,” the scientific consensus remains clear: sustainable fat loss requires consistent lifestyle changes. Weight reduction occurs when the body consistently uses more energy than it receives from food. This energy imbalance encourages the body to break down stored fat for fuel.
Certain beverages, such as green tea, coffee, or herbal infusions like ginger tea, may slightly influence metabolism or appetite. For example, caffeine can temporarily increase metabolic rate, and certain plant compounds may modestly affect fat oxidation. However, these effects are small and temporary.
The impact of these drinks is minimal compared with factors such as total calorie intake, dietary composition, physical activity, sleep quality, and stress levels. Even the most studied beverages associated with metabolism provide only modest benefits.
This is why relying on “fat-melting drinks” often leads to disappointment. The body’s metabolism is influenced by many interacting systems, and no single beverage can override them.
What actually helps reduce body fat in a safe and sustainable way?
According to Dietitian Priyanka, long-term fat loss is achieved through consistent lifestyle habits rather than quick remedies. Scientific evidence consistently shows that healthy fat loss involves a combination of sustainable behavioural and nutritional strategies. These include consuming balanced meals that provide adequate protein, fibre, vitamins, and minerals while maintaining a calorie intake appropriate for one’s energy needs.
Regular physical activity also plays an important role. Exercise increases energy expenditure and helps preserve muscle mass during weight loss. Maintaining muscle is essential because muscle tissue helps support a healthy metabolic rate.
Sleep and stress management are also increasingly recognised as important factors. Poor sleep and chronic stress can disrupt hormones that regulate appetite and metabolism, making weight management more challenging.
Replacing sugary beverages with herbal drinks such as ginger tea can certainly be a healthy habit, as it reduces added sugar intake and provides hydration. However, ginger tea should be viewed as a supportive addition to a healthy lifestyle rather than a miracle solution.

New Delhi, March 8 (IANS) Several beneficiaries and attendees expressed gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi after his rally in the Burari area of the national capital, highlighting the benefits of government welfare schemes, particularly the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana.
Among those who interacted with the Prime Minister was Shobha Devi, a beneficiary who shared how the Ayushman Card helped her receive crucial medical treatment. A heart patient, she said, the expenses for her treatment were becoming overwhelming before she received assistance under the scheme.
Speaking to IANS, she said, “PM Modi personally handed over the card to us and spoke with us. We are very thankful to him, recalling her interaction with the Prime Minister. She added that the Ayushman Card had provided significant financial relief and enabled her to continue her treatment without worrying about mounting medical costs.
Another attendee at the rally praised the Prime Minister’s initiatives for the public, especially women. “PM Modi has given wholeheartedly to the people, and he has done even more for women,” the attendee said.
Sharing a similar experience, another participant highlighted how the health scheme helped their family during a medical emergency. “My mother’s treatment was done through the Ayushman Card. The hospital bill was around Rs 1,09,000, and it was completely free of cost for us,” the attendee said.
A woman attendee said receiving benefits from the government on International Women’s Day made the moment even more special. “We feel very fortunate that we received this gift, and that too on Women’s Day. He has done so much work for people,” she said.
The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, launched by the government in 2018, is the world’s largest publicly funded health assurance scheme. It provides health coverage of up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalisation to economically vulnerable families, helping millions access affordable healthcare across the country.

New Delhi, March 9 (IANS) Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday that India’s Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) are opening new opportunities for the pharmaceutical, healthcare, and medical technology sectors, while enabling the country to strengthen its position in global trade.
Addressing the post-Budget Webinar 2026 on ‘Sabka Saath Sabka Vikas: Fulfilling Aspirations of People’, Goyal said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India has signed a total of nine Free Trade Agreements in the last three to three-and-a-half years, of which five have been concluded in the past 12 months. As a result, nearly two-thirds of global trade is now open to India.
He noted that these agreements provide India with preferential access, with lower duties and expanded market opportunities, thereby opening new avenues to enhance trade.
Goyal said that Free Trade Agreements are linked not only to large industries but also to farmers, fishermen, MSMEs, small industries, and traders. He added that these agreements benefit sectors such as pharmaceuticals and the med-tech sector that manufactures medical equipment, and also open new global opportunities for those working in innovation and emerging technologies. Highlighting India’s strong presence in the pharmaceutical sector, he said the country is widely recognised as the “Pharmacy of the World”.
He said that the benefits of Free Trade Agreements will be realised only when businesses and institutions actively utilise them. While the government can open pathways and create opportunities, trade and business must ultimately be driven by industry. Goyal said that India must build a comprehensive healthcare ecosystem that brings together manufacturing, innovation, startups and hospitals. Such an integrated ecosystem will enable the country to fully utilise the opportunities created through FTAs.
He added that MSMEs will play a significant role in this process, particularly in quality upgradation. According to him, strengthening quality standards and testing facilities will ensure that products exported from India enhance the Brand India image and showcase the country’s capabilities globally.
He said that India already has agreements or ongoing negotiations with major economies and regions, including the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand, as well as with the four European Free Trade Association countries — Switzerland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Iceland. Agreements have also been concluded with the United Arab Emirates and Oman in the Gulf region, while all six countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council have expressed interest in entering into agreements with India. He added that discussions with Canada are progressing rapidly, while talks are also advancing with Mercosur countries in Latin America and with the Eurasian Economic Union.
Goyal said that the growing global interest in strengthening trade relations with India reflects the recognition of India’s economic potential. He noted that the Indian economy, currently valued at around $4 trillion, could grow to nearly $30 trillion in the next two to two-and-a-half decades, presenting a historic opportunity for global economic engagement.
The minister emphasised the need to connect the healthcare sector more strongly with exports. He said that India should focus on training skilled professionals such as caregivers and nurses, for whom there is significant demand both in India and internationally. By strengthening skill development, India can build a workforce that supports exports, increases remittances and facilitates the global presence of Indian products and services.

Bhopal, March 9 (IANS) Under the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA), a district hospital in Madhya Pradesh’s Burhanpur district conducted health check-ups and counselling session for 40 pregnant women at its OPD.
The programme provided guidance to pregnant women on the maternal and new-born health, nutrition, and timely check-ups.
At least four high-risk cases were also identified and were subsequently given due medical advice as well as prescribed drugs for special care.
Helpline numbers were also shared for support.
The PMSMA, a dedicated service for pregnant women was started by the Central government with an objective to provide fixed-day, free-of-cost, assured, comprehensive, and quality antenatal care on the ninth day of every month, universally to all pregnant women in their second/third trimesters of pregnancy, at the designated public health facilities by government obstetricians or medical officers.
In the Burhanpur district, the health camps were organised under the aegis of Chief Medical Officer (CMO) and the Civil Surgeon.
A total of 40 pregnant women underwent prenatal physical and mental health check-ups.
District Officer Seema David told IANS, “Today marks the observance of the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan. This Abhiyan is conducted every month on the 9th and 25th at district, community, and primary healthcare levels. It focuses on specialised health check-ups for pregnant women…”
During the check-up, four pregnant women were identified as having a severe pregnancy, and their families and health workers were advised to take special precautions and maintain regular monitoring.
They were also provided with information on the importance of physical and mental health during pregnancy, timely check-ups, nutrition, and care for the mother and newborn during and after delivery.
A couple of beneficiaries expressed gratitude to the Narendra Modi-led Union government for the support, which they believe, has brought decline in infant mortality rates and promoted the concept of safe and secure pregnancy.
A family of beneficiary said, “We bring pregnant women here for ANC check-ups. If anaemia is detected during these check-ups, measures are taken so by the next visit.”
A couple of helpline numbers were also issued by the authorities, including toll-free numbers 080-47093146/47, Suman Helpline 9098640869, Suman Sakhi WhatsApp 9770905942, and Tele-Manas Helpline 14416.

Jabalpur, March 9 (IANS) Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav on Monday addressed a gathering at a programme organised as part of Fit India Women’s Week 2026 in Jabalpur, where he highlighted women’s empowerment, preventive healthcare initiatives, and ongoing development works in the state.
Speaking on women’s health, the Chief Minister praised the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, which provides the Gardasil vaccine free of cost to adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
He noted that the vaccine, which typically costs around Rs 9,000 in private clinics, is now available without charge through this drive, offering lifelong protection with just one dose.
Chief Minister Yadav commended the campaign for helping prevent future risks of cervical cancer and urged families to ensure eligible girls benefit from it.
He emphasised the government’s commitment to women’s welfare, pointing to schemes such as Ladli Behna Yojana and Ladli Laxmi Yojana.
He said that earlier daughters faced numerous challenges from birth, but these initiatives have transformed their status, making them Ladli Laxmi.

If you’ve ever stood in your kitchen, spatula in hand, wondering whether your everyday cookware could be harming your health, you’re not alone. Over the years, non-stick pans have quietly shifted from being a kitchen convenience to a source of unease, especially for women.
Social media posts and alarming articles often suggest that chemicals from non-stick cookware can “leach into food”, disrupt hormones, and even increase the risk of ovarian cancer. For many women, this fear cuts deep. Ovarian cancer is serious, often silent in its early stages, and anything linked to it naturally raises anxiety. But concern does not always equal evidence.
We will explore where the worry around non stick pan health risk comes from, what studies actually show, and how much weight this risk truly carries compared to other, more established factors.
What exactly is in a non-stick pan that raises health concerns?
Most traditional non-stick pans are coated with a material commonly known as Teflon. Its scientific name is PTFE, and under normal cooking conditions, it is considered stable and non-reactive. The concern does not really centre on PTFE itself.
Instead, attention has focused on a chemical called PFOA, which was once used during the manufacturing process of non-stick coatings. PFOA belongs to a larger family known as PFAS, often called “forever chemicals” because they break down very slowly in the body and environment.
- It can interfere with hormone regulation
- It can accumulate in the body over time
- High levels of exposure have been linked to certain cancers
PFOA has been phased out globally for over a decade. Most non-stick pans sold today are clearly labelled PFOA-free, meaning this particular chemical is no longer part of the process.
Is there real scientific proof linking non-stick pans to ovarian cancer?
At present, there is no strong, direct scientific evidence showing that cooking on non-stick pans increases the risk of ovarian cancer.
Some large studies examining PFAS exposure have found links to cancers such as kidney and testicular cancer, particularly in people exposed to very high levels, like factory workers or communities with contaminated water supplies.
When it comes to ovarian cancer, the evidence is far less clear.
- Human studies show limited and inconsistent findings
- Most data comes from populations with much higher exposure than typical home cooking
- Everyday use of modern cookware contributes very small amounts, if any
In other words, while PFAS exposure as a broad environmental issue deserves attention, non-stick cookware itself has not been proven to be an ovarian cancer trigger.
Does overheating or damaging a non-stick pan make it unsafe?
This is where practical kitchen habits matter. Non-stick pans are designed for low to medium heat. Problems arise when:
- An empty pan is heated on a high flame
- The coating is badly scratched or peeling
At very high temperatures, non-stick coatings can release fumes that irritate the respiratory tract and cause flu-like symptoms. These effects are uncomfortable, but they are not linked to cancer development.
As for scratched pans, small coating particles may mix with food, but PTFE passes through the digestive system without being absorbed. The bigger issue is functionality, not toxicity. Replacing heavily damaged cookware is sensible, not because of cancer fear, but because worn pans simply don’t perform well anymore.
How much exposure actually comes from cookware compared to daily life?
This part often changes perspective. For most people, non-stick pans are not a major source of chemical exposure. Larger contributors include:
- Certain cosmetics and personal care products
When researchers assess non-stick pan health risk, they look at dose and duration. Occasional, low-level exposure from modern cookware is minimal compared to these everyday sources.
Risk is rarely about a single item. It is about cumulative exposure across many areas of life.
Are hormonal balance and lifestyle more important than cookware choice?
Very much so. Ovarian cancer risk is influenced far more strongly by factors such as:
Lifestyle patterns that disrupt hormonal stability deserve closer attention. Repeated weight cycling, often called yo-yo dieting, has been linked to inflammation and hormonal fluctuations. Research discussing the dangers of yo-yo dieting and negative effects of yo yo dieting suggests it may influence estrogen regulation and metabolic health. There is also ongoing interest in whether yo yo diet affect endometriosis, a condition tied to chronic pelvic inflammation.
These internal factors carry far more biological weight than the type of pan used for cooking.
So, It’s natural to want control over health risks, especially when they feel close to home. But when it comes to cookware and ovarian cancer, the evidence simply does not support panic. Cooking mindfully, eating consistently, avoiding extreme dieting patterns, and supporting long-term hormonal health will protect you far more than switching pans out of fear. Sometimes, the most powerful health decision is choosing clarity over anxiety.

Your child may need extra love and care due to the discomfort caused by the pain after vaccination. Hence, in the domain of paediatric medicine, minimising the pain associated with vaccinations is paramount to ensuring a positive experience for both children and their parents. Employing diverse relief approaches can considerably mitigate the discomfort associated with vaccinations. These approaches not only promote better outcomes but also contribute to a more positive overall experience.
Hence, parents must speak with their child’s doctor about the management of pain after vaccination to ensure their child’s immunisation process is comfortable. Such open communications might help in addressing and clarifying the vaccine-associated concerns and misconceptions, respectively.
This is because vaccines play a critical role in the protection of your child; leaving them is not an option. Parents might also make use of additional resources and support networks for managing pain after vaccination.
By using these pain-relieving techniques, medical professionals can lessen the anxiety that comes with shots for kids and their parents, which will ultimately lead to better patient experiences. Therefore, this article discusses why the process of vaccination induces pain, the duration of vaccine discomfort in kids, the most painful paediatric vaccines, and methods for minimising pain after vaccination in children.
Why is there pain after vaccination in children?
Vaccines have been essential in halting the spread of infectious diseases. Vaccines stimulate the immune system to develop antibodies against particular bacteria or viruses, not the disease itself. There are several reasons why getting vaccinated could be uncomfortable:
- Vaccine needle pricks may lead to localised tissue injury that activates pain receptors in the skin and the underlying tissues.
- Vaccines may cause irritation and discomfort when the vaccine fluid gets into the muscle or subcutaneous tissue.
- The body’s immunological reaction may intensify the pain by generating inflammatory mediators.
That being said, the pain brought on by vaccinations is often minor and temporary, with variable thresholds.
How long does a vaccine’s pain last in a baby?
The duration of pain experienced by a baby during vaccination is typically short-lived, lasting only a few moments during the injection itself. Nonetheless, some kids may continue to feel pain or soreness at the injection site for a day or two following the vaccination.
When compared to the buttocks, the traditional vaccination site, infants now receive intramuscular injections in the anterior lateral thigh because vaccine shots merely cause pain after injection in the buttocks, but the site does not support the production of an effective immunological response. However, vaccination in the thigh region may also cause toddler leg pain after vaccination.
As previously mentioned, there is usually little discomfort associated with this, and it usually goes away on its own without the need for special care. Parents and other carers give the infant consolation and assurance both during and after the immunisation procedure.
If the discomfort persists or worsens, it is advised to seek further evaluation and guidance from your doctor. Overall, while some babies may experience temporary discomfort following vaccination, it is typically mild and transient, and the long-term benefits of vaccination in protecting against serious diseases far outweigh the temporary discomfort experienced.
Which is the most painful vaccine for babies?
The perception of pain can vary among individuals, but certain injectable vaccines are commonly associated with more discomfort for babies. Vaccines such as whole-cell DPT, MMR, and pneumococcal-C-13 might lead to increased local reactions and discomfort at the injection site. Additionally, several factors contribute to the perception of pain; these include the technique, length, and gauge of the needle.
While painless vaccinations for babies are available, they cannot completely replace traditional vaccinations due to their unavailability for all infectious diseases and their high costs.
When vaccinating a baby, how can you relieve their pain?
Reducing pain after vaccination is a critical aspect of a child’s healthcare. Fortunately, there is a three-P strategy that includes pharmacologic, physical, and psychological methods. These customised approaches can help alleviate discomfort and make the vaccination experience more positive for children. Hence, the recommendations have been categorised based on the requirements of infants, toddlers, and school-going children.
First and foremost, the parent or carer should hold the infant in a comfortable position, ensuring skin-to-skin contact. The likelihood of inadvertent falls is reduced when a parent stands up against the examination table to assist their child. The infant may occasionally benefit from being placed in a supine posture.
During the vaccination process, mothers should be encouraged to breastfeed their children during the vaccination procedure due to the natural pain-relieving properties.
Breastfeeding is viewed as a multimodal analgesic strategy since the acts of sucking, skin-to-skin contact, sweet-tasting milk, and holding the child can all lower pain responses. Breastfeeding should commence before the shots, continue during, and last for a few minutes after the final dose. It is necessary to install a strong enough latch before administering the vaccination.
Sweet-tasting oral solutions: For newborns, both oral sweet-tasting or sucrose-containing solutions and non-nutritive sucking work as analgesics. The underlying mechanisms for this analgesic impact include the release of endogenous opioids and distraction.
It should be stressed that sweet-tasting treatments are exclusively for newborns who do not receive breast milk at the time of vaccination. Nonetheless, breastfeeding is a better option because:
- First, breastfeeding is the preferred method of infant feeding.
- Second, there is no additional cost or training associated with breastfeeding for mothers.
- And most importantly, breastfeeding is a type of multimodal pain management.
For toddlers, distraction and comfort measures are frequently helpful. When vaccinating a toddler, parents should hold the child comfortably and securely on their laps to help ease the child’s fear and suffering.
Parental strategies: A distraction that a parent initiates or supervises is known as a parent-led distraction. Before using parent-led distraction, parents must usually undergo age-appropriate distraction training. Distraction therapy plays a role in reducing anxiety and discomfort by employing toys, bubbles, or books.
Nonetheless, a toddler’s handling during vaccination is inadequate without parental coaching. Some parenting approaches, such as nonprocedural talk, coping skills counselling, and humour, have been associated with a reduction in pain after vaccination in children. Therefore, it is essential to instruct the parents verbally, in writing, or via electronic means.
Children who attend school could benefit from more interactive pain management strategies. Pain perception can be lessened by teaching them deep breathing techniques, using topical anaesthetics, administering cold compress therapy to the injection site, and providing prescribed antipyretics.
Topical anaesthetic application: Parents should be encouraged to use topical anaesthetics during their child’s vaccinations in order to minimise suffering throughout the procedure. This method requires that parents know the precise spot or sites where the vaccination is to be administered. Application of these topical preparations 20 to 60 minutes before the vaccination is necessary, depending on the kind of commercial product. It is also important to cover them with a dressing to prevent them from being inadvertently wiped off the skin or consumed.
Tummy Breathing: Breathing exercises utilise readily available, reasonably priced things found in vaccination settings. Distracting toys and hobbies might help with slow, deep breathing or blowing. This may facilitate the child’s practice of “tummy breathing,” which involves inhaling deeply and exhaling out slowly. This distractive and calming strategy might relieve your child’s fear and anxiety during the process of vaccination.
Application of cool ice packs: Short-term and guided application of ice packs on the skin can provide a cooling sensation that can help reduce the pain associated with vaccinations. Cool ice packs are commonly available and reasonably priced. Still, they might not be useful in any circumstance.
Rewarding the child: Never tell a child that “it won’t hurt,” as this could cause the child to lose trust in you. Alternatively, children’s fear and anxiety during the vaccination treatment may be reduced by providing positive reinforcement, such as compliments and rewards, for their courage during the procedure.
It may be difficult to manage pain after vaccination in children if the parent and the medical practitioner are not actively involved. The World Health Organisation offers the following recommendations that doctors might implement to help kids feel less discomfort after vaccinations:
- Injecting the least painful vaccine formulation;
- Stroking or applying pressure to the area around the injection site before and during the injection;
- Ensuring that the child sits up or that the parent holds their baby;
- Injecting the least painful vaccine formulation first when two vaccines are being given consecutively during a single office visit;
- And quickly administering an intramuscular vaccine without aspiration
Pain relief is enhanced by combining different approaches to pain management. Therefore, it is recommended that medical experts employ a range of strategies for managing pain after vaccination. Parents, in turn, can help integrate and coordinate many of these strategies. For instance, parents can prepare their child by calming them down, bringing their toys to the visit, and encouraging deep breathing. Therefore, by integrating age-appropriate techniques with comfort measures, both parents and doctors may ensure that children receive the necessary vaccinations with the least amount of discomfort and fear.

Poliovirus, an enterovirus, can potentially cause a debilitating condition referred to as poliomyelitis. Any one of the three closely related poliovirus strains—P1, P2, and P3—can induce the illness. The poliovirus spreads from person to person through oral contact with the saliva or faeces of an infected individual. Once viral replication has been established on the mucosal surfaces of the nasal part of the pharynx, the poliovirus can multiply in specialised cells in the intestines and enter the bloodstream to infiltrate the central nervous system, where it travels along nerve fibres. Once the virus spreads inside the nervous system, it can damage motor neurones, which are nerve cells that govern skeletal muscles.
The damaged nerve cells lead to acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) that is unable to repair, and the affected muscles exhibit a lack of nerve enervation. Patients with poliomyelitis typically experience more muscle weakness in their legs than in their arms. More severe paralysis of the abdominal, thoracic, and trunk muscles can result in quadriplegia. In the most severe cases (bulbar polio), the poliovirus targets the motor neurones in the brain stem, causing respiratory difficulties as well as difficulties swallowing and speaking. In the absence of respiratory support, bulbar polio can be lethal. While it can strike anyone at any age, children under the age of three account for nearly 50% of cases.
Due to the severity of the disease in May 1988, the World Health Assembly, which is the governing body of the World Health Organisation (WHO), decided to completely eradicate polio during its annual conference in Geneva. The primary objective of the global eradication initiative is to prevent the spread of the poliovirus globally and to implement strategies to impede its reintroduction. In light of the disease prevention of this dangerous illness, this article covers all the essential aspects of the polio vaccine.
What exactly is polio vaccine? What are its different types?
A polio vaccine protects against poliomyelitis, a highly contagious viral illness that primarily affects young children. Types of polio vaccines include the oral (painless formulation) and the injectable, inactivated form.
Oral Poliovirus vaccine (OPV): Several manufacturers worldwide develop trivalent OPV utilising World Health Organisation-provided Sabin vaccine seeds, with the exception of Pfizer’s polio Sabin type 3. The oral version of the POLIO SABIN vaccination contains live, attenuated polio viruses from the type 1 (LS-c, 2ab), type 2 (P712, Ch, 2ab), and type 3 (Leon 12ab) Sabin strains stabilised with magnesium chloride.
Furthermore, each dose of OPV contains traces of less than 25 µg of antibiotics, including neomycin and streptomycin. Preservatives and adjuvants are not added.
Vaccines that have been live-attenuated are very successful in preventing the transmission of infectious viruses and in protecting against disease. Nevertheless, developing live-attenuated vaccinations that are both safe and efficacious has proven to be a challenging process of trial and error. The OPV vaccine is an excellent example of a live-attenuated vaccine that works.
Inactivated injectable polio vaccine (IPV): Similar to OPV, the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) is composed of three poliovirus strains: Mahoney type 1, MEF-1 (Middle East Forces) type 2, and Saukett type 3. The IPV is given by an injectable route. The viruses for this preparation are cultured in human diploid (MRC-5) or Vero cells before being condensed, purified, and formaldehyde-inactivated.
The Indian Academy of Paediatrics states that the polio vaccine schedule in India depends on the vaccine’s type:
The Indian Academy of Paediatrics states that the polio vaccine schedule in India depends on the vaccine’s type:
Injectable polio vaccine contains all three virus serotypes (PV1, PV2, and PV3). It is given at the age of 6 and 14 weeks, with the OPV boosters. IPV is frequently given in conjunction with DPT, Hib, and Hepatitis B vaccines.
The oral polio vaccine, which comes in a bivalent formulation with serotypes 1 and 3, is administered orally as drops. Although they are accessible, monovalent (containing only one kind) OPVs are not frequently used. The government has reserved them to address the outbreak scenarios. Two drops of OPV are given straight into the mouth.
According to the Government of India’s UIP schedule, it is advised to take one dose of OPV shortly after delivery, three more doses at six, ten, and fourteen weeks of age, and a booster at sixteen to twenty four months. Additionally, it is utilised in supplementary vaccination initiatives, also known as Pulse Polio Days.
It is important to emphasise that children who have had IPV/OPV vaccinations should receive OPV on all “Pulse Polio” days until they are five years old. While IPV is the recommended vaccine, in case it is not easily accessible or available, the kid should receive three doses of OPV at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age. Moreover, in such cases, the child should be referred to a government facility for two fractional IPV shots at the six- and fourteen-week mark.
Do these vaccines for poliovirus pose a risk?
The two vaccines for polio are both well tolerated. However, there is a rare possibility that OPV might result in vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP), especially in newborns receiving the shot for the first time. Furthermore, this live attenuated vaccine may regain its virulence and transmissibility in low-vaccine populations, increasing the risk of vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs), which have been linked to outbreaks. In addition, aseptic meningitis and encephalitis have occasionally been documented following OPV, especially in immunocompromised newborns.
Please be informed that these concerns are rare; OPV can be given in conjunction with other vaccinations, and there is no evidence that there is a decrease in immunogenicity or an increase in adverse event rates. Due to the common administration of the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DPT) vaccine concurrently with OPV, side effects from the latter are frequently confused with OPV. The immune responses to OPV have not been altered by the concurrent administration of rotavirus vaccines. However, the antibody levels to rotavirus vaccines were generally lower when OPV and rotavirus vaccinations were given concurrently. This is particularly noticeable after the first dose of OPV.
Nevertheless, OPVs have certain benefits. The oral polio vaccinations are safe, effective, and provide individuals with long-lasting protection against the targeted serotype or serotypes. Furthermore, the OPVs are reasonably priced. The primary benefit of the oral vaccine is that, following administration, the vaccine virus multiplied in the gut and may have even spread to close contacts, causing passive immunisation. Most significantly, there is no requirement for medical staff, sterile needle syringes, or an elaborate cold chain infrastructure in order to administer oral polio vaccines.
Due to this, OPVs are simple to transport to difficult-to-reach locations and to give during widespread immunisation programs.
The inactivated poliovirus vaccine is thought to be reasonably safe. However, localised responses, such as injection site erythema, induration, and discomfort, are frequently observed with IPV. These are usually short-lived, mild responses. Most of the time, they go away on their own in two or three days and don’t need to be addressed anymore.
Certain polio vaccine formulations contain trace quantities of streptomycin, polymyxin B, and neomycin, which may cause allergic reactions in certain people. However, post-marketing surveillance has not revealed any evidence of such reactions. There have been no instances of transverse myelitis, thrombocytopenia, or anaphylaxis.
Who is not eligible for the poliovirus vaccine?
OPV should not be administered to children whose immune systems have been compromised by illnesses such as HIV or who are on medications like long-term high-dose steroids or immunosuppressive therapies, nor to people who have experienced a serious allergic reaction to an earlier dose of the vaccine, such as anaphylaxis, or who have a known, severe allergy to any aspect of the vaccine.
Indian Polio Vaccine Implementation Initiative: A Success Story
The polio vaccine in India has played a crucial role in the eradication of the viral infection. On October 2, 1994, India launched the Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme, at a time when India was responsible for almost 60% of all polio cases worldwide. After 20 years of waiting, India was officially declared “polio-free” by the World Health Organisation on March 27, 2014. The last case of polio was reported in Howrah, West Bengal, on January 13, 2011.
Eradication became possible when everyone, especially the most vulnerable and marginalised people residing in the most remote areas of the nation, had fair access to vaccinations. A strong commitment at all levels resulted in legislators, medical professionals, frontline staff, partners, and community volunteers cooperating to provide every kid with life-saving polio drops wherever they were—at home, in school, or while on travel.
Apart from ensuring universal vaccination coverage, the government endeavoured to tackle social and cultural concerns to eradicate vaccine apprehension in regions with inadequate healthcare infrastructure, as well as in marginalised and susceptible communities. This was accomplished by engaging the help of local leaders and communities.
On January 31, 2021, the inaugural Polio National Immunisation Day (NID) was observed as part of ongoing efforts to maintain the nation free of the disease. As a result, vaccinations were administered in around 700,000 booths on Polio Ravivar, also known as Polio Sunday, in 2021. These booths were staffed by about 1.2 million vaccinators and 180 000 supervisors. Volunteers and partners from Rotary, UNICEF, WHO, and other civil society groups supported these workers.
In order to preserve population immunity against wild poliovirus and to maintain its polio-free status, India continues to host one National Immunisation Day (NID) and two Sub-National Immunisation Days for polio each year. To provide even more protection, the Indian government has added the injectable inactivated polio vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule.

When blood sugar drops too low, the body doesn’t whisper for help, it sends loud signals. Shaky hands. Sudden sweating. A racing heart. Foggy thinking. For some people, it can escalate quickly into confusion or even collapse. This state is called hypoglycaemia, and when it happens, time matters.
One response is almost always the same, whether at home, in an ambulance, or in a hospital ward: give glucose. Not protein. Not fats. Not “healthy snacks”. Just glucose.
But why glucose, every single time? What makes it so special during a low blood sugar episode? To understand that, we need to look at what the body, and especially the brain, goes through when glucose levels fall. Don’t worry, we’ll keep this simple, practical, and grounded in real medical knowledge.
What really goes wrong in the body during hypoglycaemia?
Glucose is the body’s main source of energy, but for the brain, it is non-negotiable. The brain cannot store glucose for later use. It depends on a steady supply from the blood, every moment of the day.
When blood sugar starts dropping, the body reacts quickly. Stress hormones like adrenaline kick in, trying to protect the brain. That’s why people feel sweaty, shaky, anxious, or unusually hungry. These symptoms are not random,they are warning signs.
If glucose continues to fall, the brain begins to struggle. Thinking slows down. Speech may become slurred. Coordination worsens. In severe cases, seizures or unconsciousness can occur. At this point, the issue is clear: the brain is running out of fuel.
And the fastest way to fix that problem is to give the fuel it needs most, glucose.
Why is glucose chosen instead of other sugars or foods?
It’s tempting to think, “Sugar is sugar, won’t anything sweet work?” In reality, it’s not that simple. Glucose has one big advantage: it doesn’t need to be broken down. Once taken, it moves straight into the bloodstream and starts raising blood sugar almost immediately.
Other sugars, like table sugar or milk sugar, need digestion first. That extra step costs precious time during hypoglycaemia. Artificial sweeteners don’t raise blood sugar at all, so they’re completely ineffective in this situation. From a medical point of view, glucose is used because it is:
When blood sugar is dangerously low, there’s no room for guesswork.
How does glucose help the brain recover so quickly?
The brain is extremely sensitive to low glucose levels. That’s why hypoglycaemia symptoms can come on suddenly and feel intense. Once glucose enters the bloodstream, it crosses into the brain using special transport systems that do not require insulin. This is crucial. Even if too much insulin causes hypoglycaemia, glucose can still reach brain cells without delay.
As soon as the brain’s energy supply is restored, symptoms often improve rapidly. Confusion clears. Strength returns. The person starts feeling like themselves again. This quick turnaround is one of the strongest reasons glucose remains the first-line treatment.
Why aren’t protein, fats, or ‘healthy’ foods used during a low?
This is one of the most common mistakes people make. Foods rich in protein or fat, like nuts, oils, ghee, or nut butters, are nutritious, yes. But they are slow. They take time to digest and do very little to raise blood glucose quickly.
Even worse, fat can slow down stomach emptying . That means any glucose taken alongside it may be absorbed more slowly, delaying recovery.
In hypoglycaemia, the goal is not balanced nutrition. The goal is speed and safety. That’s why medical guidelines clearly advise against using fats or protein for immediate treatment. These foods may be useful later, once blood sugar has stabilised, but not during the low itself.
Why is acting quickly during hypoglycaemia so important?
Hypoglycaemia is not just uncomfortable, it can be dangerous if ignored. Delayed treatment increases the risk of falls, accidents, seizures, and in severe cases, brain injury. Those early warning signs are the body asking for help. Responding quickly with glucose prevents the situation from escalating. In many ways, glucose isn’t just treatment, it’s protection.
So glucose is the gold standard when it comes to hypoglycaemia because it does exactly what the body needs, exactly when it needs it. It restores blood sugar quickly, feeds the brain directly, and reverses symptoms before they become dangerous.
Understanding this helps prevent confusion and harmful practices. In moments of low blood sugar, glucose isn’t just helpful, it’s essential.
